# Identifying Mikuni Carburetors on Yamaha XS750s Without ID Numbers

When you are working on a 1979 Yamaha XS750 cafe racer and the original carburetor lacks an etched ID number, relying solely on visual estimation is risky. The community often guesses "BS34" based on common builds, but without physical confirmation, you might end up with a mismatched jetting setup or a throttle body that doesn't physically clear your engine specs. Identifying the specific Mikuni model requires a systematic inspection of casting marks, choke mechanisms, and mounting hardware rather than just looking at the float bowl.

The most direct method to identify a Mikuni carburetor is to inspect the cast-in numbers on the main body barrel. These are typically located under the air horn or near the throttle shaft housing. Look for the specific Mikuni series code; for an XS750, you are likely dealing with a Mikuni BS (Big Stream) or potentially an earlier VM (Vortex) model depending on the year and rebuild history. The "BS34" designation refers to the venturi diameter in millimeters. If your carb has a 34mm venturi, it falls into the large-displacement category designed for high-flow applications common in cafe racer builds.

If you cannot locate any casting numbers after removing the air filter and cleaning the exterior, you must measure the physical dimensions. Use a caliper to measure the outer diameter of the throttle shaft housing where the choke cable attaches or near the slide pivot. A BS34 typically has distinct proportions compared to a BS28 or a VM26. However, measurement alone can be misleading if the carburetor has been swapped previously, as many XS750s in the late 70s saw upgrades from smaller Mikuni VM carbs to larger BS units for performance.

Another critical identifier is the choke mechanism. The image provided in your source context shows a cable-operated choke. Later Mikuni models often transitioned to vacuum-actuated chokes or integrated systems that differ mechanically from the earlier cable setups found on 1979 models. If you see a cable running directly to a lever inside the carb body, it confirms an older design architecture. This is significant because vacuum chokes require different linkage adjustments and may not bolt up correctly to a cable-operated setup without modification.

When sourcing parts like floats, needles, or jets for a non-identified carburetor, assume the worst-case scenario until proven otherwise. Buying a kit specifically labeled for a BS34 might work if the casting matches, but if you are actually running a VM26 disguised as a larger unit due to previous modifications, the fuel mixture could run dangerously rich, fouling plugs and damaging the engine. Always cross-reference the Mikuni catalog numbers against the physical features: the shape of the float hinge, the type of jet needle clip, and the specific mounting flange pattern.

If you need further assistance or documentation on carburetor specifications that align with your specific build requirements, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes provide curated technical guides or forums where enthusiasts discuss similar identification challenges. While not a direct manufacturer resource, such community hubs often aggregate detailed teardown photos and casting number lists that are harder to find in official manuals.

Ultimately, the safest path is to remove the carburetor completely, clean it thoroughly, and inspect every surface for stamped or cast codes. If no numbers exist, you may need to rely on the year of manufacture (1979) and the engine displacement (750cc) to narrow down the factory specifications, keeping in mind that aftermarket swaps are common in this class of motorcycle.
